Palladium-catalysed alleneamination of $\gamma .$ d-unsaturated hydrazones with propargylic acetates: access to tetrahydropyridazines bearing allenes†
Shuaijie Wu,<sup>a</sup> Shiji Xu,<sup>a</sup> Yanru He,<sup>a</sup> Jing Sun,<sup>a</sup> Wei Jiang,<sup>b</sup> Chao-Guo Yan, \*<sup>a</sup> Weiming Hu \*<sup>c</sup> and Lei Wang \*<sup>a</sup>

A highly eficient palladium-catalysed alleneamination of c, d-unsaturated hydrazones with propargylic acetates has been developed. This novel method was used to synthesize tetrahydropyridazines bearing allene derivatives, and did so in moderate to good yields. This protocol features a simple catalytic system, broad substrate scope, easy scale-up, and versatile transformations.

Tetrahydropyridazines constitute a class of six-membered N-heterocycles and represent a privileged motif in various natural products.<sup>1</sup> Moreover, tetrahydropyridazines and their derivatives exhibit a large range of pharmacological activities,<sup>2,3</sup> such as neuro-transmitter inhibitor, antimicrobial, influenza neuraminidase inhibitor, and cannabinoid CB receptor activities. In addition, they play an important role in synthetic organic chemistry as versatile building blocks due to the presence of an N–N bond (Fig. 1).<sup>4</sup> Therefore, the development of efficient synthetic methodologies for their preparation has attracted considerable attention.

Over the past two decades, significant eforts have been devoted to developing elegant routes toward six-membered nitrogen-containing heterocycles, including hydrogenation of pyridine<sup>5</sup> and aza-Diels–Alder reactions (Scheme 1a).<sup>6</sup> Hydrazones are key structural motifs and have been widely used in drug development, materials science, and biological probes. Meanwhile, the advantages of hydrazones, including their easy preparation, the presence of an N–N bond, and their role as synthetic equivalents to ketones or aldehydes enables their extensive use for synthesizing a range of N-heterocycles.<sup>8–10</sup> Especially, the hydrazones containing unsaturated C–C double bonds have been frequently studied for the synthesis of tetrahydropyridazines. For instance, Xiao’s, Liu ’s and Stuart’s group independently realized the synthesis of functionalized tetrahydropyridazines through 6-endo-trig cyclization (Scheme 1b, left).<sup>9</sup> Afterwards, the Yu and Pan group developed a similar method that produced sulfonylated tetrahydropyridazines in moderate to good yields (Scheme 1b, right).<sup>10</sup> In addition, the Chen and Xiao group<sup>11</sup> in 2017 described Pd(II)-catalysed aminoarylation reactions of g,d-unsaturated hydrazones, providing general approaches to tetrahydropyridazines. Later, Zhang and Zhao reported an efficient Pd(0)-catalysed cyclization-coupling reaction of readily available g,d-alkenyl hydrazone with organohalides for the synthesis of tetrahydropyridazines (Scheme 1c).<sup>12</sup> Despite these achievements, additional efforts for their efficient synthesis are highly desirable.

Allenes are useful building blocks for the synthesis of pharmaceuticals, natural products, and functional materials.<sup>13,14</sup> A variety of methods for the eficient synthesis of diferent kinds of allenes have been well developed.<sup>14</sup> Transition-metal–catalysed reactions of propargylic alcohol derivatives with various reagents represent one of the most useful and efficient methodologies for synthesizing allenes (Scheme 1d).<sup>15</sup> In this context, we set out in the current work to develop an efficient palladium-catalysed alleneamination of $\gamma , \delta \mathrm { - }$ unsaturated hydrazones with propargylic acetates, leading to the formation of allene-containing tetrahydropyridazines (Scheme 1e).

text: We initiated the present study with the investigation of $\gamma ,$ d-unsaturated hydrazone 1a (0.2 mmol, 1.0 equiv.) and propargylic acetate 2a (0.4 mmol, 2.0 equiv.) as starting materials in the presence of Pd catalyst (10 mol%) and phosphine ligand (12 mol%) (Table 1). When a mixture of 1a and 2a in THF (2.0 mL) was treated with 10 mol% of $\mathbf { P d } ( \mathbf { c o d } ) \mathbf { C l } _ { 2 }$ and 12 mol% of $\mathrm { P P h } _ { 3 }$ in the presence of 1.5 equiv. of <sup>t</sup>BuOK as a base at $5 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ under argon for 24 h, the reaction proceeded smoothly to give the desired product 3a in 42% yield (Table 1, entry 1). Then, a series of phosphine ligands, such as XPhos, DpePhos, and RuPhos, were tested (Table 1, entries 2–4). Fortunately, the yield of 3a improved to 73% when XPhos was used as the ligand (Table 1, entry 2). Afterwards, we tested for the effects of various palladium catalysts including $\mathrm { { \bf P d } } _ { 2 } ( \mathrm { d } \mathrm { b a } ) _ { 3 } , \mathrm { { \bf P d } } ( \mathrm { O A c } ) _ { 2 } , \mathrm { { \bf P d C l } } _ { 2 } ,$ and [Pd(allyl)Cl] , but no better result was observed (Table 1, entries 5–8). Replacing KO<sup>t</sup>Bu with other bases such as $\mathrm { K } _ { 2 } \mathrm { C O } _ { 3 } , \mathrm { N a O } ^ { t } \mathrm { B u }$ and $\mathrm { C s } _ { 2 } \mathrm { C O } _ { 3 }$ led to significant decreases in the yields (Table 1, entries 9–11). Other solvents such as toluene, CH CN, 1, 4-dioxane, and DCE were further screened, but the product 3a was obtained with unsatisfactory results (Table 1, entries 12–15). When the reaction was performed under an air atmosphere, only a trace amount of the product 3a was obtained. Moreover, no product 3a was obtained in the absence of a ligand (Table 1, entry 17). Finally, we found that the reaction efficiency did not decrease at all when the reaction was carried out on a scale of 0.3 mmol (Table 1, entry 18).

With the optimal reaction conditions in hand, we investigated the generality of $\gamma , 8 \cdot$ -unsaturated hydrazones 1 reacting with 2a in the current method as shown Scheme 2. As expected, a wide range of g,d-unsaturated hydrazones 1 bearing diferent groups on the aryl ring—both electron-donating groups including methyl, phenyl, and tert-butyl groups and electronwithdrawing groups including fluoro, trifluoromethyl, and cyano groups—were well tolerated, yielding the corresponding allene-bearing tetrahydropyridazines 3b–3h in moderate to good yields (46–79%). Notably, disubstituted and heterocyclesubstituted substrates also reacted smoothly to deliver 3i–3l in yields ranging from 46% to 67%. Furthermore, $\gamma , 8 \mathrm { - }$ unsaturated hydrazones bearing alkyl groups, such as isopropyl, cyclohexyl, and cyclopropyl, exhibited lower reactivity, and the products 3m–3o were produced in only 32–48% yields. In addition, styrylsubstituted product 3p was obtained, in 47% yield. Unfortunately, primaryl alkyl, benzyl, and disubstituted alkene motif substrates were not compatible, and 3q–3s were not formed at all. Additionally, the configuration of 3a was confirmed by the results of X-ray diffraction.<sup>16</sup>

text: Next, the scope of propargylic acetates 2 was investigated by reacting them with 1a (Scheme 3). Regardless of the electronic nature of the para-substituents on the aryl ring, functionalized propargylic acetates reacted well with hydrazone 1a and produced a range of allene-containing tetrahydropyridazine derivatives 4a–4g with good results (50–79% yields). When the substituents were located at a meta- or ortho-position, the desired tetrahydropyridazine products formed successfully, although steric effects could not be ignored (4h, 77%; 4i, 41%). Furthermore, 2-naphthyl, cyclohexeyl, cyclopropyl, and heterocycles like thiophene and quinoline were well tolerated, affording products 4j–4n in 42–70% yields. Interestingly, the propargylic acetates bearing a cyclic system were also applicable to the current transformation, and the desired products 4p–4r were afforded in 50–73% yields. To demonstrate the potential applications of this method, fenofibrate derivative propargylic acetate were also tested, which produced the desired coupling product 4s in 55% yield.

text: To prove the practicality of this approach, a gram-scale reaction was attempted. A 5.0-mmol-scale reaction of $\gamma ,$ d-unsaturated hydrazone 1a with propargylic acetate 2a proceeded smoothly, afording 1.19 g of 3a with an acceptable yield of 66% (Scheme 4a). The potential applicability of the system was further illustrated by the good results of the transformations of 3a, such as a 5-endo cyclization reaction with TfOH and oxidation of the allene group (Scheme 4b). In addition, the use of a KMnO oxidation system allowed allene 3a to be used to form ketone 6 in 77% yield.

On the basis of the previous reports and the experimental results,<sup>17</sup> a plausible reaction mechanism is proposed (Scheme 5). First, the oxidative addition of propargylic acetates to Pd(0) generates a Pd(II) complex II. Subsequently, deprotonation of 1a and ligand exchange give intermediate III, which then undergoes a migratory insertion to provide complex IV (path a). Alternatively, coordination of alkene to Pd(II) complex II afords III<sup>0</sup>, followed by attack of alkene by the deprotonated hydrazone moiety to obtain intermediate IV (path b). Finally, reductive elimination of complex IV afords the corresponding product 3a, and regenerates the Pd(0) catalyst for the catalytic cycle.

text: In conclusion, we developed an eficient palladiumcatalysed alleneamination reaction, which provides an eficient and practical approach for the synthesis of allene-bearing tetrahydropyridazines in moderate to good yields. A variety of readily available g,d-unsaturated hydrazones and functionalized propargylic acetates as starting materials demonstrated good tolerance. This protocol features a simple catalytic system, a broad substrate scope, easy scalability, and versatile transformations. Further investigation on the asymmetry of the transformation is currently underway.
